subject: Samhällskunskap
title: Society and the individual
sourceSummary: What a society is and how you as an individual are shaped by it — the family and different family forms, groups and peer pressure, norms and values, and how identity develops.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a society?
questions.opener: Think about what is needed when many people are going to live together in the same place.
choices: A group of people who live together and share common rules, tasks and activities
A single house where one family lives
A company that sells goods to customers
A sports club with a board
questions.explanation: A society is many people living together who need to organise themselves with shared rules and activities, such as schools, healthcare and police. A company or a club, on the other hand, exists inside society — they are parts of it, not the whole society.

questions.prompt: Which statement about family forms in Sweden is most accurate?
questions.opener: Think about how many different ways a family can look among the people you know.
choices: Only a mother, a father and their children count as a family
All families in Sweden have exactly two adults
Families can look many different ways, for example a nuclear family, a single parent, a blended family, or two parents of the same sex
The municipality decides which family form you should have
questions.explanation: In Sweden there are many family forms: nuclear families, single parents, blended (step-) families, families with two mothers or two fathers, and families where relatives are involved. Only counting the nuclear family as a family therefore does not match how things actually look.

questions.prompt: What is meant by peer pressure?
questions.opener: Is it about what you yourself want, or about what others expect of you?
choices: That a group lobbies politicians to change a law
That someone does something they would not otherwise do, because others in the group do it or expect it
That a teacher divides the class into groups
That you always feel good about being part of a group
questions.explanation: Peer pressure is when the group's expectations control a person's actions more than the person's own will. A group trying to influence politicians is instead lobbying — something quite different from peer pressure between individuals.

questions.opener: The difference from a law is that a norm is not written down anywhere.
choices: A law decided by parliament
A fine you have to pay if you do something wrong
An opinion that only one single person holds
An unwritten rule for how you are expected to behave
questions.explanation: A norm is an unwritten rule, for example greeting people when you enter a room or standing in a queue. Laws, on the other hand, are written rules decided by parliament that can lead to punishment if broken — breaking a norm usually only leads to reactions from others.

questions.opener: The word is about how we learn to function in society, not about hanging out in your free time.
choices: That you spend a lot of time with friends at weekends
The process by which we learn society's language, norms and roles through family, school, friends and media
Moving to a new country
The state deciding what profession you should have
questions.explanation: Socialisation is the long process by which a person learns how society works — language, norms, values and roles. Spending time with friends is part of socialisation, but the concept itself means the learning, not the socialising itself.

questions.prompt: What is the group that a person belongs to and feels a sense of community with called?
questions.opener: The term is the opposite of an "out-group".
choices: Out-group
Formal authority
Minority
In-group
questions.explanation: The group you belong to yourself is called an in-group, and groups you place yourself outside of are called out-groups. Dividing people into "us" and "them" can create a sense of community, but can also create prejudice against those who end up in the out-group.

questions.prompt: Some classmates want you to join in writing nasty comments about another student. Describe step by step how you can think through handling the situation.
questions.opener: Start by putting into words what is happening, then think about who is affected.
questions.answer: First you establish that this is peer pressure: you feel pressure to do something you don't actually want to do. Then you think about who is affected — the student being targeted, but also yourself if you take part. You weigh your options: joining in, saying no, walking away, or telling an adult. You test the choice against your own values and ask yourself how you yourself would want to be treated. Finally, you choose not to join in, and tell a teacher or another adult if it continues, since online harassment can be both against school rules and against the law.
steps: Name the situation: this is peer pressure, not your own decision.
Think about who is affected — the person being targeted, the group and yourself.
List your options: joining in, saying no, walking away, or telling an adult.
Test the options against your own values: how would you want to be treated?
Choose not to join in, and tell an adult if it continues — the school is obliged to stop harassment.

questions.prompt: Summarise the basic concepts of society, the group and the individual.
questions.opener: Go through society, family, group, norms and identity as five short points.
questions.answer: Society: many people living together with shared rules and activities such as schools, healthcare and police · Family forms: nuclear family, single parent, blended family, two parents of the same sex, relatives as guardians — all count as families · Group: a primary group is close and personal (family, friends), a secondary group is more impersonal (the class, the team, the workplace) · In-group and out-group: the division creates a sense of community but can also create prejudice · Peer pressure: doing something for the sake of the group's expectations instead of your own will · Norm: an unwritten rule for how you are expected to behave · Value: what a person or group considers important and right · Law: a written rule decided by parliament, can lead to punishment · Socialisation: the process by which we learn language, norms and roles — the family first, then school, friends and media · Identity: the perception of who you are, shaped throughout life by background, interests and the groups you belong to.
